newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks spooked by Fed interest-rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks spooked by Fed interest-rate hike.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks closed lower Tuesday as Wall Street reacted nervously to the Federal Reserve's interest rate hike, a move that could slow the economy and dampen corporate profits.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 29.08 points at 6,876.17. But in the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,295 to 1,161 on active volume of 480 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

In a widely anticipated move, the Fed raised the key federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point to 5.50 percent - the first increase since Feb. 1, 1995 -- in an effort to stay a step ahead of inflation.

Some commercial banks wasted no time reacting to the Fed's tightening. Citibank, Banc One Corp. and Central Fidelity Bancorp raised their prime lending rates to 8.50 percent from 8.25 percent, which will eventually boost the lending rates for home equity loans, adjustable mortgages and credit cards.
Blue chips initially jumped on the Fed's decision, which was announced at mid-afternoon but the so-called "relief rally" quickly evaporated.
Traders said that even though the market had expected the Fed to raise rates, there was some concern that this might be the first in a series of hikes.
"It's still a bump in rates and maybe there's another bump to come," said Frank Calta, director of trading at Anvil Institutional Services.
Added Eric Miller, chief investment office at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, "Once the Fed has signalled a change in policy, it means the market should be on its guard."
Wall Street will be closely following economic indicators to determine if more credit tightening is in the offing.
"I would guess the market is going to mark time, stay in a trading range until it gets a better sense of what is going to follow," Miller said.

In the bond market, the key 30-year Treasury bond lost more than one-half point, sending its yield up to 6.97 percent from Monday's close of 6.92 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
"If (the Fed) does a second (rate hike), that's when people will get nervous," said Kevin Haggerty, manager of equity trading at Fidelity Capital Markets.
Meanwhile, technology stocks rebounded after a recent battering, buoyed by comments from Montgomery Securities that it viewed the shares of major tech companies as undervalued.
Intel Corp. rose 2-5/8 to 133-1/4, Cisco Systems Inc. gained 3/4 to 47-7/8 and Dell Computer Corp. rose 2-1/2 to 67-1/2.
Drug stocks rallied after Morgan Stanley raised its rating on Warner-Lambert Co., which gained 1-3/4 to 91-1/4, Eli Lilly & Co. rose 2-1/2 to 89-1/4 and Merck & Co. added 1-1/8 to 91.
Drug stocks are among consumer non-durable shares normally seen outperforming other stocks in a slowing economy.
Bank and other economically sensitive stocks, seen vulnerable to rising rates and a slower economy, were weak.
Banc One fell 1 to 43-3/4 and Citicorp shed 7/8 to 115-3/4. Aluminum Co. of America dropped 2 to 70.

One cyclical sector, paper stocks, fell after Merrill Lynch lowered its ratings on the group, citing pricing pressures on some products. Weyerhaeuser Co. fell 2-1/4 to 46-3/4, Georgia-Pacific Corp. sank 2-1/2 to 73-7/8 and Champion International Corp. fell 1-3/4 to 45-1/4.
Among special situations, Global DirectMail Corp. fell 8-1/8 to 19-7/8 after it warned of disappointing results.
Motorola Inc. rose 1-1/2 to 58-7/8 on expectations that the company will announce a major contract with a Japanese wireless phone company.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 5.42 points to 1,248.06.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 1.82 to 789.07. The American Stock Exchange index slipped 1.78 to 586.16.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.59 to 415.41. The average share was down 6 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,497.325 down 4.118 or 0.05 percent.
